title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Systematic evaluation of variability in large language model (LLM)-generated outputs is critical for assessing their reliability. We developed a general statistical framework and Python package (llmReproScore) for quantifying the repeatability and reproducibility of LLM outputs. Following US Food and Drug Administration terminology, our framework establishes four metrics for quantifying LLM repeatability and reproducibility along two dimensions: semantic and internal. Semantic metrics quantify variability in the meaning of LLM-generated outputs, whereas internal metrics quantify variability in token-generation certainty. We validated these metrics, and as an illustrative use case, applied them to diagnostic reasoning outputs generated across LLMs and prompting strategies using US Medical Licensing Examination questions and 90 real-world rare disease cases from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. Validation results showed that semantic scores aligned with human ratings (Spearman ρ = 0.88 for repeatability and 0.66 for reproducibility) and confirmed that internal metrics capture variability in token-generation certainty. In the illustrative use case, LLM repeatability was generally not associated with accuracy, suggesting that LLM output variability and accuracy capture distinct dimensions of model performance. The proposed metrics can be used to characterize LLM output variability and systematically compare models, prompts, and generation settings. These comparisons can inform more rigorous selection of LLM configurations based on repeatability and reproducibility. We developed and validated generalizable metrics for quantifying LLM output variability. The proposed metrics can complement accuracy-based evaluation to inform experimental design and support more rigorous comparison and selection of models, prompts, and generation settings.

title: Automated Radiation Target Contouring and Treatment Planning Via RATA: A Multi-Center RCT
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: zhaoxiaohui; conditions: Cancer, Malignant Neoplasms, Radiotherapy; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 62; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Radiotherapy, a cornerstone of comprehensive cancer treatment, relies heavily on clinician expertise for target volume contouring and treatment planning. Consequently, clinical practice is often constrained by procedural bottlenecks, inter-observer variability, and prolonged iterative feedback cycles. Although current artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated progress in automated contouring, key limitations persist, including insufficient integration of multimodal clinical text, a lack of closed-loop dosimetric feedback, and limited generalizability across complex cancer types. This study aims to develop and validate RATA (Radiotherapy Treatment Multi-Agent Assistant), a novel large model system powered by a collaborative multi-agent architecture. Driven by Large Language Model (LLM) decision engines, RATA processes pathological imaging, electronic health records (EHR), and multimodal medical data to construct a end-to-end, fully automated closed-loop pipeline encompassing "target contouring, plan design, dosimetric evaluation, and reflective refinement." Innovatively breaking through traditional unidirectional radiotherapy workflows, the system establishes a dosimetric feedback-driven adaptive iteration mechanism, leveraging dose distribution outcomes to guide multi-agent dynamic fine-tuning of target volumes, thereby mimicking the collaborative clinical logic between senior radiation oncologists and medical physicists. For validation, this study adopts a multi-center, three-stage clinical validation framework-comprising multi-center retrospective validation, human-AI collaborative efficacy assessment, and a prospective randomized controlled trial (RCT)-to comprehensively evaluate the system's performance in improving contouring precision, mitigating experience-dependent disparities across clinician seniority, and reducing total workflow processing time. Implementation of the RATA platform holds potential to eliminate redundant operational steps, enabling a minute-level "scan-to-treat" response. Furthermore, its natural language interaction interface optimizes human-AI collaboration and substantially reduces clinical workload. Overall, this study not only establishes a standardized, intelligent assistance paradigm for precision radiation oncology but also provides essential evidence-based support and technological foundations for the clinical translation of multimodal AI in complex cancer management.

title: Patient-Friendly Simplifications of Outpatient Reports Using Large Language Models via Few-Shot Prompting: Blinded Comparative Evaluation.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Effective communication between clinicians and patients plays an important role in the successful delivery of health care. In geriatric medicine, where multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and functional limitations often make treatment plans complex, AI simplifications of clinical reports into patient-friendly language offer a promising way to improve communication. This study investigated whether AI could generate patient-friendly simplifications of outpatient reports that were comparable to those authored by human experts. Gemma-3-27B-it, an instruction fine-tuned open-source large language model (LLM) by Google, was used, and few-shot prompting was applied to enable the generation of patient-friendly simplifications of 64 deidentified geriatric outpatient reports written in German while preserving clinical meaning. LLM-generated simplifications were compared with those produced by 2 medical experts in a blinded evaluation. Quality was assessed using three approaches: (1) embedding-based semantic similarity to the original report, (2) blinded expert review by 2 clinicians, and (3) review by patient representatives, with the latter 2 using a standardized Likert-scale questionnaire. AI-generated simplifications were comparable to geriatrician-authored simplifications regarding semantic similarity (P=.02) and were preferred by patient representatives (P<.001) as well as one expert reviewer (P=.001). Expert reviewers perceived physician-authored simplifications as more complete (P<.001), a finding that correlated with text length (P<.001). This study demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs via few-shot prompting to simplify medical reports for improved perceived patient comprehension in geriatric care. Future prospective studies should examine whether such AI-driven simplifications positively impact objective health-related outcomes, adherence, and patient engagement.

title: SphereFlow: Missing Modality Imputation via Geometric Transport on Hypersphere
desc: Missing modality imputation aims to synthesize unobserved modalities from observed ones. Existing methods treat each modality as living on its own latent manifold, forcing the generator to learn a long, unstructured jump between them. We present SphereFlow, which takes a fundamentally different view: by projecting all modalities into a shared hyperspherical latent space via a frozen self-supervised encoder, cross-modal imputation reduces to short-range geometric transport between nearby points on the sphere. Realizing this idea with flow matching, however, exposes two geometric conflicts: the standard Gaussian noise source is catastrophically mismatched with the unit-norm data manifold, and the linear interpolation path departs the sphere surface into a region where the decoder has no training signal. We resolve both with simple, geometry-aware modifications: replacing the noise source with the observed-modality latent so that the velocity field learns only the cross-modal displacement, and training the decoder with a time-weighted loss that extends its domain to the near-surface region traversed by the flow. We prove that this data-as-source formulation reduces the worst-case off-manifold deviation from a quantity that grows with the latent dimension to a small, dimension-independent bound governed by inter-modality similarity. Experiments on BraTS multi-modal MRI imputation and CT-MRI translation demonstrate state-of-the-art generation fidelity across all settings, while downstream brain tumor segmentation with our imputed data closes roughly eighty percent of the gap to the full-modality oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/WTHH031230/SphereFlow.

title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
desc: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection

title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
desc: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

title: Organotchi: an open-source tool for the automated segmentation, morphological characterization, and longitudinal tracking of organoids
desc: Neural organoids are three-dimensional stem cell-derived models widely used to study brain development and model disease. Brightfield imaging offers a non-invasive readout of their growth and morphology, and recent advances have made automated organoid segmentation from such images increasingly attainable. Yet existing tools largely leave morphological characterization, quality assessment, and comparisons between conditions to manual or ad hoc analysis. Here we present Organotchi, an open-source tool that integrates automated segmentation with longitudinal morphological analysis of neural organoids. Organotchi quantifies ten morphological features, including area, perimeter, and eccentricity, and tracks cystic structures over time, reports variability within and between batches, and flags outlier organoids and segmentation failures, supporting objective organoid characterization and enhancing downstream analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply Organotchi to disease modelling, pharmacological perturbation, and protocol optimization in neural organoids. One use case assesses drug response in breast cancer spheroids, demonstrating its use beyond its development domain.

title: Unimodal imaging foundation models and vision-language models in MRI: A systematic review of emerging methods and clinical applications.
desc: [Cell reports. Medicine] Artificial intelligence in medical imaging is shifting from task-specific algorithms toward adaptable foundation models (FMs) and vision-language models (VLMs). However, applying these models to MRI remains challenging because clinical interpretation requires integrating multi-parametric, volumetric imaging across multiple sequences with clinical context. This systematic review evaluates 35 studies on unimodal FMs and multimodal VLMs in MRI, summarizing emerging architectures, downstream applications, and challenges to clinical translation. Current research is concentrated in neuroimaging, with diagnostic classification representing the most mature application. Segmentation and outcome prediction also show promise, whereas automated report generation remains limited by poor clinical fidelity despite strong linguistic fluency. Broader adoption is hindered by heterogeneous MRI acquisition, limited large-scale paired image-text datasets, and inadequate safety-focused evaluation metrics. Advancing clinical translation will require standardized multicenter datasets, stronger integration with electronic health records and pathology, robust evaluation frameworks, and improved model explainability.

title: Evaluation of an AI-Assisted Tool for CLABSI Surveillance at VA Medical Centers
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Maryland, Baltimore; conditions: Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI), Bacteremia, Bloodstream Infections; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 30; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Infection prevention and control programs at US hospitals perform surveillance to detect and publicly report hospital-onset central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) using standards set by CDC's National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN). Because this process requires time-consuming review of the medical record by dedicated infection preventionists, VA has developed a generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool that applies the NHSN CLABSI standard to clinical data from the medical record. In this quality improvement initiative, we will evaluate the tool as it is implemented operationally across a cohort of VA medical centers in 3 randomized waves. The purpose of this evaluation is (1) to determine whether the tool reduces the time required for CLABSI surveillance, (2) to assess the objectivity and trustworthiness of the tool from the perspective of infection preventionists, and (3) to detect patient safety events.

title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
desc: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
desc: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

title: An explainable, bias-audited machine learning model to detect hidden hepatitis C from region-wide real-world health records
desc: Background: Although direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee [≥]60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded [≥]30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. Results: In the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. Conclusion: An explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
desc: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.
